title: Urinary organic acid analysis in preventive health assessment and healthy-aging research: A state-of-the-art review of evidence and methodological limitations

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Urinary organic acid analysis in preventive health assessment and healthy-aging research: A state-of-the-art review of evidence and methodological limitations》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · p0010】Advances in preventive health assessment increasingly emphasize the need for biomarkers capable of capturing functional metabolic alterations before the manifestation of overt disease [1], [2]. In this context, metabolomics investigates metabolic changes associated with genetic predisposition, environmental exposures, nutrition, lifestyle, and host–microbiome interactions [2], [3].

【Introduction · p0015】As part of these metabolic profiling approaches, the analysis of organic acids in urine has been proposed as a functional readout of intermediary metabolism. Urinary organic acids represent end products and intermediates of multiple biochemical pathways, including carbohydrate metabolism and glycolysis (e.g., lactate, pyruvate), amino acid catabolism (e.g., phenylpyruvate, α-ketoisovalerate), fatty acid β-oxidation and lipid metabolism (e.g., adipate, suberate), and mitochondrial energy metabolism within the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle (e.g., citrate, succinate, fumarate, malate), as well as microbial-derived or host–microbiome co-metabolites (e.g., hippurate, p-hydroxybenzoate) [4]. Chromatographic–mass spectrometric methods are used to measure urinary organic acids, with gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC-MS) widely employed in clinical testing for inherited metabolic disorders [5]. Foundational work describing the composition and diversity of the human urine metabolome has provided an essential basis for subsequent applications of urinary metabolomics in human research [6].

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Urinary organic acid analysis in preventive health assessment and healthy-aging research: A state-of-the-art review of evidence and methodological limitations》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Methods · p0030】The present research is a state-of-the-art narrative review of UOA measurements and related urinary metabolomic evidence, including their potential relevance to preventive and aging research. A narrative approach was selected to integrate heterogeneous clinical and methodological evidence, discuss current developments, and identify knowledge gaps and future research directions [13], [14], [15].

【Analytical methods, normalization, and quality assurance · p0090】GC-MS is widely used in clinical organic acid analysis for inherited metabolic disorders [4]. Research investigations may employ GC-MS, liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC-MS), capillary electrophoresis–mass spectrometry (CE-MS), or nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), with targeted or untargeted measurement strategies. Instrument choice alone does not establish metabolite coverage, quantitative accuracy, or fitness for clinical use, and methodological standardization remains essential for comparability [2]. For targeted quantitative assays, validation should address the intended analytes, calibration, selectivity, precision, accuracy, reportable range, and relevant matrix effects [21]. Untargeted workflows require documented quality control, analytical reproducibility, and transparent reporting of metabolite identification or annotation [22].

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Urinary organic acid analysis in preventive health assessment and healthy-aging research: A state-of-the-art review of evidence and methodological limitations》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【External validation and clinical relevance · p0275】The examples above support biological investigation rather than established preventive or healthy-aging applications. External validation of a multi-omics prediction model requires evaluation of a prespecified model in an independent population for a defined outcome, including assessment of discrimination and calibration [68]. Internal cross-validation, replication of individual associations, or external validation of a metabolomics-only model should not be described as external validation of an integrated multi-omics model. External validation has been reported for a broader urinary NMR age model developed in 4184 participants and evaluated in an independent cohort of 3701 participants [43]. This illustrates external validation of a urinary metabolomics model, but does not establish external validation of a multi-omics model or an organic-acid-specific assay [43].

【External validation and clinical relevance · p0280】Future studies should establish whether adding urinary organic acids improves prediction beyond conventional clinical variables and the other molecular layers, rather than relying on statistically significant associations alone [69]. For proposed applications in aging research, this requires longitudinal evaluation against meaningful outcomes, such as incident frailty or functional decline, with appropriate consideration of renal function and other determinants of urinary excretion. Predictive performance should also be distinguished from clinical impact: prospective comparative studies are needed to determine whether using a model improves clinical decisions and patient outcomes [70].

【Fig. 2 · fig2】Fig. 2 Evidence-informed framework for urinary metabolomics and multi-omics integration in preventive health assessment. The figure summarizes selected investigations included in Table 3. Clinical interpretation requires consideration of renal function, population characteristics, and sampling conditions [16], [42], [65]. Microbiome studies link urinary metabolites with microbial diversity and composition [17], [51]. Metabolomic investigations report associations with metabolic phenotypes, renal outcomes, and aging-related characteristics [8], [32], [34], [39], [40], [43]. Complementary urinary proteomic and metabolomic investigations address aging and mitochondrial disease [52], [63], while genetic analyses inform urinary metabolite variation and renal handling [16]. The molecular layers represent separate study-specific investigations, not a single externally validated multi-omics model. The segmented tube is a schematic organizing device and does not imply that all molecular measurements were obtained from urine.
